strengths: Moving Out is a timely and potentially useful benchmark. It combines continuous control, 2D physics, heterogeneous objects, narrow passages, and coordination, awareness, and action-consistency scenarios that are largely absent from standard grid-world benchmarks.
The human-human dataset is nontrivial: over 1,000 demonstrations from 36 participants for behavioral diversity and 720 demonstrations from four experts under randomized object properties.

BASS is a sensible combination of partner-behavior augmentation and model-based action selection. With the diffusion-policy backbone, it substantially improves AI-AI completion metrics: Task 1 TCR rises from 0.3829 to 0.5027 and NFD from 0.4818 to 0.5707; Task 2 TCR rises from 0.3125 to 0.4348 and NFD from 0.4526 to 0.5535.

The evaluation includes AI-AI and human-AI interaction, component ablations, an oracle-simulator comparison, qualitative failure analysis, map descriptions, computational costs, and real-time inference measurements.

The paper is generally readable and visually communicates the environment well. It reports IRB approval and participant compensation, and its limitations section appropriately acknowledges restricted physical coverage, inference-speed constraints, and persistent failure cases.
weaknesses: The human-study account is materially inconsistent. Section 6.1 reports 32 participants, each playing 32 maps with both methods and role swapping; Appendix I reports 12 volunteers, each selecting one of four model IDs and playing 12 maps. These represent different sample sizes and experimental designs, making the central human-AI evidence unreliable as written.

The human-study statistics are inadequate. The paper reports a single p=0.017 from unspecified “independent t-tests,” without identifying the outcomes, sample size, test statistics, confidence intervals, or correction across nine questionnaire items. The described within-participant design appears to require paired or repeated-measures analysis. Figure 7 has no uncertainty intervals, and numerical human-AI results are not tabulated.

The task protocols are underspecified. For Task 1, no demonstration train/validation/test split is defined, participant overlap is not addressed, and “unseen human strategy” is not operationalized. For Task 2, the distributions and ranges of mass, size, and shape and the precise train/test partition are absent, so the claimed out-of-distribution physical generalization cannot be audited.

BASS is not reproducible from the manuscript. It omits the number and generation procedure for candidate actions, particularly for deterministic MLP/GRU policies; leaves the partner-action predictor application-dependent; and lacks losses, weights, optimization details, augmentation volume, and dynamics-model sampling details. The project-page link is blank, with no actionable code or data availability statement.

The trajectory-recombination justification is unsound. Matching one agent's start and end cells on a 48x48 grid does not ensure that a substituted partner trajectory is compatible with the original object and environment trajectory. It may create collisions, inconsistent grasps, or impossible object transitions. The method performs no validity check and does not quantify invalid samples, despite describing the generated trajectories as valid.

Several claims overstate the results. Full DP+BASS worsens Task 1 waiting time from 0.3075 to 0.3448, where lower is better, and barely changes Task 2 action consistency from 0.8442 to 0.8474. For GRU on Task 2, full BASS has lower TCR than the no-augmentation variant, 0.3414 versus 0.3670. MLP plus augmentation reduces TCR in both tasks. No statistical analysis supports repeated claims of significant AI-AI improvements.

The learned dynamics model is weakly validated: selected-action agreement with the oracle is only 0.625 for Task 1 and 0.487 for Task 2, without the candidate count or a chance baseline. One-step ranking by immediate NFD provides limited evidence of understanding longer-horizon constraints such as grasping, rotation, and navigating passages. The one-sentence Overcooked result lacks protocol and uncertainty and does not establish generality.

Baseline fairness is unclear. MAPPO uses heavily engineered dense and map-specific rewards, including special geometry for Map 11, while tuning budgets, training-seed variability, and uncertainty are not reported. Relevant partner-modeling, offline/model-based imitation, and zero-shot coordination methods are discussed but not evaluated.

Formal and editorial inconsistencies reduce precision: the Dec-MDP formulation mixes decentralized observations with joint full observability; the objective is written as an unweighted sum rather than an expectation; and the transition is called deterministic while expressed as sampling. Other inconsistencies include NDF/NFD, BAAS/BASS, and Task 1 DP+BASS NFD values of 0.5707 in the main ablation versus 0.5733 in the oracle appendix.

The benchmark has promising originality and significance, but the contradictory human-study protocol, undefined generalization splits, incomplete method specification, and unsupported augmentation validity are major soundness and reproducibility problems that prevent acceptance in its current form.

strengths: The Moving Out benchmark addresses a useful problem: human-AI cooperation under continuous control, collisions, object properties, and sustained joint manipulation. Its 12 layouts cover several recognizable coordination modes.
The authors collected substantial human-human demonstration data and attempted an interactive human-AI evaluation, which is more informative than relying exclusively on self-play.

The evaluation includes multiple behavioral metrics, component ablations, an oracle-simulator comparison, and qualitative failure analysis. The manuscript also reports IRB approval, participant compensation, computational costs, and inference speed.
BASS improves task-completion measures over the tested behavior-cloning backbones, especially with Diffusion Policy; for example, Task-2 TCR increases from 0.3125 to 0.4348.
weaknesses: Soundness: the behavior recombination procedure does not ensure physically valid trajectories. It swaps a partner subtrajectory while retaining the original agent and environment sequences, matching only discretized endpoint cells. Intermediate collisions, contacts, object states, and causal transitions can therefore be inconsistent. The paper explicitly states that it performs no validity checking, yet attributes improvements to learning diverse valid collaborative behavior.

Central experimental splits are insufficiently specified. The manuscript does not explain how Task-1 participants or trajectories are divided between training and testing, whether human-study participants overlap with data contributors, or precisely how Task-2 physical attributes are partitioned to guarantee genuinely unseen test configurations. Appendix F.1.3, titled Evaluation Setting, is empty. Consequently, the principal adaptation and generalization claims cannot be independently assessed.

The human-study reporting is internally contradictory. Section 6 states that 32 participants each played 32 maps, whereas Appendix I reports 12 volunteers selecting among four models and playing 12 maps per model. The assignment, randomization, counterbalancing, model identities, and number of observations used in each analysis are unclear.

Statistical evidence is inadequate. The objective human-AI results are shown mainly in a small plot without a numerical table, confidence intervals, or hypothesis tests. The survey reports a single p=0.017 from unspecified independent t-tests despite an apparently repeated-measures design, nine Likert questions, and multiple comparisons. This does not substantiate broad claims of significantly better human collaboration.

The Action Consistency metric does not generally measure force alignment as claimed. It projects the sum of the forces onto the vector connecting the agents; perfectly aligned forces perpendicular to that vector score zero. Thus, conclusions about synchronized action are not supported by the stated formula.

BASS is not reproducibly defined. Missing details include the dynamics and autoencoder losses, candidate-action count and sampling procedure, selection horizon, partner-predictor training and usage, normalization, augmentation quantity, and training/model-selection protocol. The project-page field is blank, and no code or data availability statement resolves these omissions.

The comparison set is weak for the claimed state of the art: it consists largely of generic MLP, GRU, Diffusion Policy, and MAPPO baselines, despite the related-work section identifying human-aware and diverse-partner coordination methods. MAPPO also receives heavily engineered dense rewards, including map-specific shaping, making its result difficult to interpret as a general baseline.

The evidence for physical understanding is limited. The learned simulator agrees with oracle-selected actions only 48.7% of the time on Task 2, and its action score uses grid-based object-to-goal distance that ignores object orientation, size, contact feasibility, and joint-manipulation constraints. Better task metrics therefore do not establish the asserted understanding of physics.

Significance is constrained by the evaluation being limited to a simplified 2D Pymunk environment, 12 layouts, and two closely related tasks. The manuscript repeatedly describes the physics as realistic and motivates embodied robotics, but supplies no evidence of transfer to richer simulators or real systems; the lone Overcooked result is only an unsupported one-sentence 15% claim.

Presentation requires substantial revision: important definitions and protocols are scattered or absent, participant counts conflict, several claims of significance lack supporting analyses, and there are numerous grammatical and typographical errors. The limitations discussion acknowledges scope and inference speed but omits the more consequential validity, statistical, and sim-to-real limitations above. These technical and evidential deficiencies presently outweigh the benchmark's promise.

strengths: Originality and significance: Moving Out is a useful benchmark concept that expands human-AI coordination beyond discrete grid worlds to continuous, physics-based interaction. Its 12 maps cover coordination, assistance awareness, joint carrying, and sustained action consistency.

The data contribution is substantial: the authors report more than 1,000 human-human demonstrations from 36 participants for behavioral diversity and 720 expert demonstrations with randomized physical properties for generalization.

BASS combines partner-behavior augmentation with learned one-step dynamics and action selection in a sensible, broadly applicable framework. Experiments with both GRU and diffusion-policy backbones generally improve TCR and NFD, and the oracle-simulator comparison helps contextualize the learned model's remaining gap.

The evaluation includes behavior cloning, diffusion, and MAPPO baselines; four task-oriented metrics; component ablations; AI-AI trials over multiple seeds; a human-AI study; subjective feedback; and qualitative failure analysis. This is broader evidence than is typical for a new benchmark.

Presentation is generally clear and visually effective. The environment, collaboration modes, task definitions, maps, metrics, computing requirements, and several implementation hyperparameters are documented in the paper and appendix.

The manuscript appropriately acknowledges limited physical-interaction coverage, inference-speed constraints, and persistent failure cases. It reports IRB approval and participant compensation, with no apparent unresolved ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness is weakened by a major inconsistency in the human-study account. Section 6.1 reports 32 participants, each playing 32 maps, whereas Appendix I reports 12 volunteers and describes selecting among four model IDs and playing 12 maps per model. This makes the sample size, experimental design, and resulting human-AI evidence impossible to determine reliably.

The human-study statistics are insufficient. The paper reports an independent t-test with a single p=0.017 despite an apparently within-subject or repeated-measures design and multiple questionnaire outcomes. It does not provide per-condition sample sizes, effect sizes, uncertainty, multiple-comparison treatment, or objective human-AI results in a numerical table. Model ordering, identity blinding, and counterbalancing are also unclear.

The trajectory-recombination augmentation is not convincingly shown to produce physically valid training data. Matching only one agent's discretized start and end cells does not ensure that the swapped partner trajectory is compatible with intermediate object states, grasps, collisions, or forces. The authors explicitly omit validity checking, yet characterize the constructed trajectories as valid and do not isolate recombination from simple pose perturbation in the ablation.

Reproducibility of BASS is inadequate. The manuscript does not specify the dynamics/autoencoder training losses and weights, how action candidates are generated or how many are evaluated, the exact partner-action predictor used in the reported experiments, or enough inference details to reconstruct the selector. The project URL is blank in the submitted manuscript, and no code or data availability statement resolves these omissions.

The train/test protocols are underspecified. Task 1 lacks the exact participant-level split and filtering criteria for the approximately 1,000 retained demonstrations. Task 2 lacks precise physical-property ranges, sampling distributions, and held-out combinations. These details are central to claims of generalization to unseen people and physical attributes.

Several conclusions are stronger than the reported evidence. Objective AI-AI improvements are not accompanied by significance tests, and full BASS is not uniformly best: for example, with DP on Task 1, waiting time worsens from 0.3075 to 0.3448, while some GRU ablations outperform the full method on individual metrics. Learned next-state action-selection agreement with the oracle is only 0.487 on Task 2.

The Action Consistency definition appears questionable: it projects the sum of forces onto the vector connecting the agents, rather than directly measuring agreement between their force directions or progress along the object's desired motion. The manuscript does not justify why this formula represents force alignment, so claims based on AC are difficult to interpret.

Overall, the benchmark and empirical direction are promising, but the conflicting human-study description, questionable augmentation validity, missing algorithmic details, and insufficient statistical reporting prevent the central human-collaboration claims from being considered technically solid enough for acceptance in the current form.

strengths: Originality/significance: Moving Out is a potentially useful benchmark for continuous, physics-mediated human–AI coordination. Its 12 maps cover coordination, assistance awareness, and sustained joint manipulation, a broader range than many discrete collaboration benchmarks.

The submission contributes sizable human–human demonstration data: more than 1,000 demonstrations from 36 participants for behavioral diversity and 720 demonstrations with randomized physical properties for generalization.

BASS is intuitive and practically motivated: it combines partner-behavior augmentation, learned one-step dynamics, and candidate-action selection. Experiments include component ablations, alternative dynamics models, an oracle-simulator comparison, sampling-cost analysis, and failure cases.

The evaluation considers partial progress, waiting, and physical coordination in addition to completion. AI–AI results generally favor BASS over the same Diffusion Policy backbone, while the oracle gap usefully indicates remaining potential.

Presentation is generally readable, visually polished, and supported by extensive appendices containing model hyperparameters, compute requirements, metric definitions, maps, and data-collection procedures.
Ethics treatment is adequate at a basic level: the authors report IRB approval and participant compensation, and the simulated domain presents limited immediate safety risk.
weaknesses: Soundness: the human-study account is internally contradictory. Section 6.1 reports 32 participants, each playing 32 maps and switching roles after the first round; Appendix R reports 12 volunteers, each selecting one of four model IDs and playing 12 maps, with roles determined by model ID. These describe materially different designs, so the central claim of superior human–AI collaboration cannot be reliably interpreted.

The human-study statistics are inadequate. The paper reports a single independent t-test p=0.017 despite an apparently repeated-measures or partially between-subject design, nine questionnaire items, two tasks, and multiple objective outcomes. It does not identify the tested outcome, provide effect sizes or confidence intervals, correct for multiple comparisons, or model participant/map effects.

Several numerical results are unexplainedly inconsistent. For example, Task 1 seen-behavior DP/BASS TCR is 0.3503 in Tables 2/14 but 0.5027 in Tables 5/15; DP is 0.3233 versus 0.3829. Tables 15–16 are nevertheless described as presenting all Task 1/2 results. Other BASS NFD values also vary across tables without clearly defined protocols. This substantially harms evidential reliability.

The subtrajectory recombination is not shown to be dynamically valid. Matching only one agent's start/end pose—approximately, after discretization to a 48×48 grid—does not ensure compatibility of the substituted partner states/actions with object states, contacts, collisions, or the retained environment trajectory. The claimed greater-than-99% validity lacks a definition, validation algorithm, sample size, or results broken down by failure type.

The learned dynamics method is underspecified: no complete training objective, reconstruction/prediction loss, loss weights, normalization, or training protocol is given. Action selection evaluates paired samples of predicted partner behavior rather than an expectation or robust criterion, so it may select an action based on an optimistic partner sample that will not occur.

The Action Consistency metric does not generally measure force alignment as claimed. It projects the summed forces onto the vector connecting the agents; two perfectly aligned forces perpendicular to that vector score zero. Consequently, AC results and conclusions about coordinated force application are difficult to justify.

Task 1's cross-group AI–AI protocol is only an indirect proxy for adaptation to unseen humans: it measures compatibility between separately trained policies, not online adaptation to a human. The limited and inconsistently documented human experiment does not fully repair this gap.

Baseline coverage and fairness are limited. BASS is primarily compared with basic behavior-cloning architectures and one reward-shaped MAPPO implementation; the paper omits stronger partner-modeling, offline-RL, planning/model-predictive-control, and contemporary zero-shot coordination baselines discussed in its own related work. MAPPO also receives map-specific dense reward engineering, making the comparison hard to interpret.

Significance is constrained by evaluation solely in a stylized 2D simulator with small physical-attribute perturbations (pose, mass, and size varied by up to 10%) and no sim-to-real or robotics validation. Claims about embodied agents and real-world use should therefore be narrower.

Reproducibility is not yet adequate: the abstract's project-page URL is blank, and no accessible code/data release, exact participant splits, random seeds, dataset filtering criterion, or per-task human-study assignment is supplied. Some implementation details are present, but they are insufficient to reproduce the central results.

The limitations discussion is too brief. It mentions inference speed and future complexity but does not address simulator-to-real transfer, the validity of recombined trajectories, demographic representativeness, the cross-policy proxy, human-study power/design, or the contradictory reporting. These unresolved evidential issues outweigh the benchmark's promise.

strengths: Significance: Moving Out targets a useful gap between symbolic human-AI coordination benchmarks and continuous, physics-mediated collaboration. The 12 layouts cover handoffs, assistance decisions, joint carrying, and constrained rotations, while the four proposed metrics capture both completion and interaction quality.

Empirical scope: The paper includes human-human demonstrations, AI-AI evaluation, a human-AI study, component ablations, oracle-simulator comparisons, prediction-error measurements, and qualitative failure cases. BASS generally improves task completion and normalized final distance over its Diffusion Policy backbone.

Presentation: The motivating examples, environment diagrams, rollout visualization, and map-by-map appendix make the intended challenges easy to understand. Computational costs and many implementation hyperparameters are reported.

Ethics: The authors state that both data collection and the user study received IRB approval and report compensation of $15–$20 per hour. The simulated, low-stakes domain raises no major immediate safety concern.
Originality: Combining partner-behavior augmentation with learned one-step dynamics and candidate-action selection is a coherent approach, even though the individual ingredients are established.
weaknesses: Soundness: The behavior-recombination argument is not valid as written. Matching only one agent's discretized start and end poses does not establish that a substituted partner subsequence is compatible with the intervening object states, contacts, forces, or environment trajectory. Likewise, perturbing the partner pose while leaving all other variables unchanged can create dynamically inconsistent samples. The claimed >99% physical validity is unsupported by a definition, protocol, or breakdown of failures.

Soundness: Task 1's cross-group AI-AI protocol is not a reliable proxy for adaptation to unseen humans. It tests interaction between two learned policies trained on different participant subsets, whose behavior distributions and correlated errors may differ substantially from those of people. Consequently, the main reproducible evaluation does not directly establish the central human-adaptation claim.

Soundness/reproducibility: The human-study description is materially contradictory. Section 6 reports 32 participants, each playing 32 maps and cooperating with each method in two rounds per map, whereas Appendix R reports 12 volunteers who select one of four model IDs and play 12 maps. These imply very different sample sizes, assignment schemes, and statistical units, so the strongest human-AI results cannot be interpreted or reproduced reliably.

Statistics: The human results provide no uncertainty estimates, per-condition sample sizes, randomization/counterbalancing details, or effect sizes. A single p=0.017 from independent t-tests is reported despite multiple questionnaire outcomes and an ambiguously paired or grouped design, with no multiple-comparison correction. Claims that BASS significantly improves both helpfulness and perceived physics understanding therefore are not adequately supported.

Experimental consistency: Results that appear to represent the same settings differ substantially without explanation—for example, Task 1 DP/BASS TCR is 0.3503 in the main seen-behavior table but 0.5027 in the ablation tables, while DP changes from 0.3233 to 0.3829. The paper does not clearly identify the different splits or protocols that would explain these numbers.

Evaluation coverage: Comparisons are limited mainly to basic behavior-cloning architectures and MAPPO. The MAPPO comparison is not well controlled because it uses hand-designed, sometimes map-specific dense rewards and no human demonstrations. More relevant partner-modeling, offline/model-based control, and zero-shot coordination baselines cited by the paper are absent.

Generalization evidence is underspecified. Task 2 does not provide the exact train/test property combinations, ranges, dataset split, or per-property results needed to determine whether success reflects compositional physical understanding rather than interpolation or map-specific behavior. Only four experts generated this dataset, further limiting behavioral coverage.

The dynamics-model evidence is incomplete: very small aggregate state-space L2 error can be dominated by easy, static dimensions and does not demonstrate accurate contacts or rare constrained transitions. Action-selection accuracy is only 48.7% on Task 2, while the policy uses a myopic one-step NFD objective, yet the paper makes broader claims about understanding physical constraints.

Originality: BASS is largely a combination of trajectory augmentation, behavioral cloning, a learned one-step transition model, and sample-and-rerank action selection. The limited comparison to related stitching and model-based planning approaches makes it difficult to establish a substantial methodological advance.

Reproducibility/presentation: The abstract says the project page is available but gives no URL, and the manuscript provides no code or dataset release link. Several important definitions remain ambiguous, including waiting-time normalization, augmentation-validation criteria, human-study assignment, data filtering, and exact Task 2 splits. There are also mathematical and editorial issues, such as an expected-return expression that omits trajectory probabilities and repeated inconsistencies between deterministic-transition claims and probabilistic notation.

Limitations and ethics treatment is too narrow. The paper briefly notes inference speed and residual failures but does not discuss simulator-to-real transfer, sensitivity to participant demographics, dependence on privileged full-state observations, risks of unreliable assistance, or privacy and release conditions for human trajectory data. IRB approval is welcome but does not replace these disclosures.

Overall, the benchmark idea and collected data are promising, but unsupported augmentation validity, contradictory human-study reporting, unclear statistical analysis, and insufficiently controlled generalization evidence undermine the paper's central claims. These are substantive evidential and reproducibility problems requiring major revision rather than minor clarification.

strengths: The paper introduces Moving Out, a useful and reasonably original benchmark for continuous, physics-based human–AI collaboration. Its 12 maps cover coordination, awareness, joint manipulation, collision avoidance, handoffs, and sustained action consistency—capabilities poorly represented in predominantly discrete benchmarks. The dataset is a meaningful contribution: Task 1 contains approximately 1,000 demonstrations from 36 participants, while Task 2 contains 720 demonstrations with randomized physical properties. The participant-disjoint and compositional generalization protocols address relevant forms of distribution shift.

BASS is conceptually straightforward but effective. Combining partner-behavior augmentation, learned next-state simulation, and candidate-action selection improves the diffusion-policy backbone on task completion and normalized progress. Under Task 1 cross-group evaluation, for example, TCR rises from 0.2563 to 0.3010 and NFD from 0.4589 to 0.5197.

The evaluation is broader than is typical for a benchmark paper: it includes four objective metrics, AI–AI and human–AI tests, module ablations, alternative dynamics models, random-partner-action and oracle-simulator comparisons, sampling-efficiency analysis, qualitative failures, and compute/inference measurements.

The oracle comparison is particularly informative: it exposes the remaining gap caused by imperfect learned dynamics, especially for Task 2, rather than presenting BASS as having solved physical generalization.

Presentation is generally clear and well organized. Figures communicate the environment and collaboration modes effectively, and the appendix supplies observation/action encodings, architectures, hyperparameters, reward definitions, metric formulas, and data-collection procedures.

The work reports IRB approval and participant compensation of $15–$20 per hour. The simulated setting presents no evident material safety concern, and the paper openly discusses persistent behavioral failures rather than concealing them.
weaknesses: The human-study reporting contains a serious internal inconsistency: Section 6.1 states that 32 participants each played 32 maps, whereas Appendix R states that the experiment involved 12 volunteers and describes four model IDs with 12 maps per model. This prevents the reader from determining the actual sample size, exposure per participant, and experimental design.

The human-study statistics are insufficiently specified and potentially inappropriate. Participants apparently evaluate multiple models, suggesting paired or repeated-measures analysis, yet the paper reports an independent t-test. It also evaluates nine questionnaire items but reports only one p-value (0.017), without identifying the exact comparison, giving uncertainty intervals/effect sizes, or correcting for multiple comparisons. Consequently, claims that multiple subjective differences are significant are not presently supported.

The human evaluation compares BASS only with its DP backbone. This supports the incremental benefit of BASS but does not establish superiority over broader human-aware collaboration approaches. Model-ID selection also appears participant-chosen rather than randomized, and blinding, order counterbalancing, attrition, and demographic information are not reported.

Task 1's reproducible cross-group proxy evaluates two learned policies against each other, not adaptation to unseen humans. Both policies inherit biases from the same model family and collection process, so this protocol can measure cross-policy compatibility without faithfully measuring human behavioral diversity. The direct human results help, but the paper overstates what the proxy alone establishes.

The augmentation validity argument is incomplete. Matching only one agent's discretized start and end cells does not guarantee that a swapped partner subsequence remains dynamically or collaboratively consistent with intermediate object states. The claimed greater-than-99% validity rate lacks a definition, evaluation procedure, and sample count; pose perturbations likewise alter observations without regenerating physically consistent transitions.

Several experimental gains have sizeable, overlapping standard errors, and results are averaged over 20 runs without clarifying whether these represent independently trained seeds or repeated rollouts of the same trained policies. Formal uncertainty or significance analysis is missing for the principal objective comparisons.

The baseline set is relatively narrow—basic MLP/GRU behavior cloning, diffusion policy, and reward-shaped MAPPO—and lacks stronger partner-modeling, offline-RL, planning, or contemporary zero-shot-coordination baselines. MAPPO additionally receives extensive map-specific reward shaping, making the comparison informative but not especially clean.

External validity remains limited to a stylized 2D simulator, 12 hand-designed maps, two agents, 10 Hz control, and modest physical-attribute changes. The single-map Overcooked result is stated without enough experimental detail to substantiate the broader claim that BASS transfers beyond Moving Out.

Reproducibility is only partial: many implementation details are supplied, but the project-page URL is blank, no code/data release is established in the manuscript, the precise train/test object combinations and random seeds are not enumerated, and exclusion of 'significantly poor' demonstrations is not governed by an explicit criterion. These issues should be fixed before archival publication.
